justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assumed was a recent price level around 335–337 for the underlying asset, likely an equity index or ETF. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price with only a small expected move, as short-term mean reversion and intraday momentum tend to dominate. At the one-week horizon, I projected a slightly higher estimate of 339, reflecting a mild positive drift assumption consistent with a modest bull bias in trending markets, while acknowledging that a week is long enough for meaningful macro news to shift the picture. At the one-month horizon, I pushed the estimate a bit higher to 342, incorporating a longer-run drift expectation while also widening the range substantially to account for the compounding of daily uncertainty over roughly 21 trading sessions.

The confidence interval widths were driven primarily by the scaling of volatility across time horizons. Daily volatility for a broad index instrument tends to run somewhere in the 0.5–1% range under normal conditions, which justified a relatively tight 90% interval of about ±9–10 points at the one-day level. As the horizon extends to a week, volatility scales by roughly the square root of time, pushing the interval wider to about ±19 points. At one month, that scaling effect produces an interval of roughly ±37–38 points, which reflects the realistic uncertainty accumulation over that period. I also gave some extra weight to tail risks at longer horizons, which is why the intervals are not perfectly symmetric around the point estimates.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these stated intervals include sudden macroeconomic shocks such as an unexpected central bank policy decision, a surprise inflation print, or deteriorating credit conditions that could trigger a sharp sell-off well beyond the lower bounds. Geopolitical escalations or liquidity crises could produce outsized moves in either direction on very short notice. On the upside, a strong earnings surprise season, unexpected dovish pivot from a major central bank, or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical tension could push prices above the upper bounds of my longer-horizon intervals.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume relatively stable volatility regimes. If realized volatility were to spike — as it does during stress events — even the one-day interval could prove too narrow. Conversely, in a very low-volatility, range-bound environment, the actual price path might stay well inside even the tighter short-horizon bounds. The one-month interval in particular carries meaningful model uncertainty, since structural regime changes or persistent trend shifts are difficult to anticipate from a baseline forecast alone.
